lead: A valve slams shut at the end of a long pipe. Water cannot stop instantly; it piles against the valve and a pressure wave races back up the pipe. That surge is water hammer, strong enough to split a main. The same physics, reversed, explains the siphon: a pipe climbs over a crest where pressure drops below atmospheric and delivers water to a lower level with no pump. Both occur in hydropower, building supply, canal irrigation and long pumping mains.
prereq: You need: bulk modulus and compressibility (see Unit 1, Fluid Properties and Fluid Statics), Bernoulli's equation (see Unit 3, Fluid Dynamics and Flow Measurement) and the 4.6 Hydraulic gradient and total energy lines.

sections.h3: Water hammer: the surge after a fast closure

blocks.text: In steady flow the valve pressure follows the hydraulic gradient. Shut the valve quickly and water at the valve stops. Water behind still moves at V and slams into the stopped slice. Pressure jumps, the pipe wall stretches, and a compression wave runs back to the reservoir at wave speed a.

At the reservoir the wave reflects as a low-pressure wave and returns. Pressure swings above and below steady value, decaying as friction eats energy. Old plumbing knocks for this reason; the name comes from the noise and the hammer-blow force on bends and valves.

Closure speed sets surge size. Let L be pipe length in m and T<sub>c</sub> the closing time in s. If T<sub>c</sub> < 2L/a, the wave returns after closure: rapid closure, full surge. If T<sub>c</sub> ≥ 2L/a, the reflected wave arrives during closing and cancels part of the rise: slow closure, smaller surge.

sections.h3: Wave speed and the Joukowsky pressure rise

blocks.where: a = wave speed in m/s; K = bulk modulus of water, about 2.2 GPa; ρ = density of water, 1000 kg/m³; D = pipe internal diameter in m; E = Young's modulus of pipe material in Pa (about 200 GPa for steel); t = wall thickness in m. K D/(E t) compares water squeeze with pipe stretch.

blocks.text: A rigid pipe (E → ∞) gives a = √(K/ρ) ≈ 1483 m/s. A thin steel wall lowers a to about 1200 m/s; a thick wall or concrete raises it.

blocks.where: Δp = surge pressure above steady pressure, in Pa; ρ = water density, 1000 kg/m³; a = wave speed from the first formula, m/s; V = velocity change in m/s, equal to full flow velocity for rapid closure. Valid only for rapid closure.

blocks.text: In head form ΔH = aV/g. A 1236 m/s wave with V = 2.0 m/s gives ΔH = 252 m. The surge adds to steady pressure, so design pressure is p<sub>steady</sub> + Δp.
Four defences: close slowly so T<sub>c</sub> ≥ 2L/a; fit a surge tank, a vertical standpipe near the valve; fit an air vessel, a trapped air pocket that cushions the surge; add a relief valve.

sections.h3: The siphon: lifting water with low pressure

blocks.text: A siphon carries water over an obstacle higher than both free surfaces, from an upper reservoir to a lower one, with no pump. Some syllabi spell it syphon. Layout: up leg, crest, down leg.

Driving head is the level difference H between free surfaces, not crest height. Bernoulli from upper surface (1) to outlet (2): H = h<sub>L</sub> + V²/2g, with h<sub>L</sub> total pipe loss in m and V outlet velocity in m/s. Gravity pulls the longer, heavier down leg and drags the up leg along.

blocks.where: p<sub>c</sub> = absolute pressure at crest, Pa; p<sub>atm</sub> = atmospheric pressure, about 101.3 kPa; z<sub>c</sub> = crest height above upper free surface, m; V<sub>c</sub> = velocity at crest, m/s; h<sub>L,up</sub> = friction loss in up leg, m.

blocks.text: The three terms after the atmospheric term are subtracted, so crest pressure is below atmospheric.

Crest pressure cannot fall below vapour pressure, about 2.3 kPa absolute at 20 °C (0.24 m of water absolute). Setting p<sub>c</sub> = p<sub>vap</sub> gives maximum crest height roughly 10.3 − 0.24 − V<sub>c</sub>²/2g − h<sub>L,up</sub> metres, in practice 6 to 8 m. Higher and water boils at the crest, the column breaks, and the siphon stops. This is the same cavitation that damages pump inlets (see Unit 7, Centrifugal and Reciprocating Pumps).

items: Priming: pipe must be full of water with no air pocket. Air at crest expands instead of pulling, column separates, nothing flows. Fill the pipe, or use a small pump or valve to drive air out.
Uses: emptying a sump or fish tank, drawing canal water over a field bund, taking water from a dam reservoir over the dam body, an emergency drain that needs no power.

figure.caption: Water leaves the upper reservoir, climbs the up leg to the low-pressure crest, then falls down the down leg to the lower reservoir. Only the level difference drives flow.

examples.question: A steel pipe of internal diameter D = 0.20 m, wall thickness t = 5 mm and length L = 500 m carries water at V = 2.0 m/s. Take E = 200 GPa, K = 2.2 GPa and ρ = 1000 kg/m³. A valve closes rapidly. Find wave speed, Joukowsky pressure rise, equivalent head and the closure time below which closure is rapid.
steps: Water alone: K/ρ = 2.2×10⁹/1000 = 2.2×10⁶ m²/s², so √(K/ρ) = 1483.2 m/s.
Critical closure time: 2L/a = 2 × 500/1236 = 0.809 s. Closure is rapid only below 0.809 s.
Surge pressure: Δp = ρ a V = 1000 × 1236 × 2.0 = 2.472×10⁶ Pa = 2.472 MPa.
examples.answer: a = 1236 m/s, Δp = 2.472 MPa (252.0 m of water head); rapid only when the valve shuts in under 0.809 s.
examples.check:
import math
K = 2.2e9
rho = 1000.0
E = 200e9
D = 0.20
t = 0.005
V = 2.0
L = 500.0
g = 9.81
a = math.sqrt(K/rho)/math.sqrt(1 + K*D/(E*t))
dp = rho*a*V
h = dp/(rho*g)
tc = 2*L/a
print(round(a,1))
print(round(dp/1e6,3))
print(round(h,1))
print(round(tc,3))

examples.question: A siphon lifts water over a crest 6.0 m above the upper reservoir. Velocity at crest is 1.5 m/s and up-leg loss is 0.8 m. Take p<sub>atm</sub> = 101.3 kPa and ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Find absolute crest pressure and state whether the siphon works.
steps: Head removed: z<sub>c</sub> + V²/2g + h<sub>L,up</sub> = 6.0 + 0.115 + 0.8 = 6.915 m.
This is far above vapour pressure (about 2.3 kPa at 20 °C), so the column stays unbroken and the siphon works.
examples.answer: Crest pressure is about 33.5 kPa absolute, well above vapour pressure, so the siphon runs without cavitation.

traps: Using Δp = ρaV for slow closure. Joukowsky holds only when T<sub>c</sub> < 2L/a; for slow closure use roughly Δp ≈ 2ρLV/T<sub>c</sub>.
Taking a = 1483 m/s for every pipe. That is the rigid-pipe value; a steel pipe gives 1236 m/s, so rigid value overestimates surge by about 20 %.
Forgetting surge adds to steady pressure. Design pressure is steady plus surge, and a 252 m surge dwarfs friction head.
Believing a siphon can lift water to any height under 10.3 m. Crest pressure must stay above vapour pressure; velocity head and up-leg friction leave about 6 to 8 m.
Thinking siphon discharge depends on crest height. Driving head is the difference between free surface levels; crest height only controls pressure there.
Sign slip: gauge pressure at the crest is negative, so crest pressure is below atmospheric, not above it.

quiz.a: The pressure surge when flow velocity in a pipe changes suddenly, as by fast valve closure or pump trip; the surge travels as a wave at speed a.

quiz.q: State the Joukowsky equation and name each symbol.
quiz.a: Δp = ρ a V, with Δp surge pressure in Pa, ρ water density in kg/m³, a wave speed in m/s, V velocity change in m/s; valid for rapid closure, T<sub>c</sub> < 2L/a.

quiz.q: Why is the surge smaller when the valve closes slowly?
quiz.a: For T<sub>c</sub> ≥ 2L/a the reflected low-pressure wave returns while the valve is still closing. It partly cancels the rise, so only part of the Joukowsky surge is reached.

quiz.q: Why must a siphon be primed before it will work?
quiz.a: Air at the crest expands easily and cannot sustain the pressure difference; the column separates and flow stops. Filling the pipe removes air so low crest pressure can pull the column over.

quiz.q: A cast-iron pipe has D = 0.15 m, t = 4 mm, E = 100 GPa. Water has K = 2.2 GPa, ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and flows at V = 1.5 m/s. Find wave speed and rapid-closure surge.
A siphon crest is 7.5 m above the upper reservoir, V at crest is 2.0 m/s and up-leg loss is 1.1 m. Find absolute crest pressure (p<sub>atm</sub> = 101.3 kPa) and check against vapour pressure.
quiz.a: Head removed = 7.5 + 2.0²/(2×9.81) + 1.1 = 8.804 m. p<sub>c</sub> = 101300 − 9810 × 8.804 = 14.9 kPa absolute, above 2.3 kPa vapour pressure, so the siphon works.

quiz.q: A valve on a 500 m pipe (a = 1236 m/s, V = 2.0 m/s) closes in 1.2 s. Is the closure rapid? Estimate the surge realistically.
quiz.a: 2L/a = 1000/1236 = 0.809 s; 1.2 s exceeds it, so closure is slow and Joukowsky does not apply. Use Δp ≈ 2ρLV/T<sub>c</sub> = 2×1000×500×2.0/1.2 = 1.67 MPa, about two thirds of the rapid-closure value.

quiz.q: How does an air vessel reduce water hammer in a pumping main?
quiz.a: Trapped air acts as a spring. Extra water pushed by the surge compresses it, and later the air pushes water back, so velocity changes gradually instead of instantly. Wave amplitude falls and pump discharge is smoothed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real surge analysis uses the method of characteristics, which marches the wave along the pipe in short time steps and adds friction at each step; Joukowsky is only a first estimate. Hydropower designers use such models for load rejection, when a turbine guide vane closes in seconds on a long penstock, and size the surge tank from the result. Useful searches: method of characteristics surge analysis, surge tank design, siphon priming, column separation.
